I lead a research group and we're starting a deep dive into reasoning methods for large language models. There's a PDF in your workspace called Survey_Guidelines.pdf that outlines the structure we want, and a guide.md with some notes on how to organize the taxonomy and comparison criteria.

I need you to search for recent papers on chain-of-thought prompting, tree-of-thought reasoning, self-consistency decoding, step-by-step verification, and automatic chain-of-thought generation. There should be several relevant papers in the database. Download and read through them to understand the key contributions and methodologies.

Once you've reviewed the papers, write a comprehensive survey document called LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx. It should follow the structure in the guidelines: start with an abstract summarizing the survey, then an introduction to the field, a background section, a taxonomy of methods section broken into subsections for each reasoning approach, a comparative analysis section with a table comparing the methods, a section on open challenges, and a conclusion. Each method subsection should reference the corresponding paper and summarize the key ideas, methodology, and results. Make sure you cover at least five distinct reasoning methods. Use proper Word heading styles (Heading 1 / Heading 2) for the section and subsection titles so the document is well structured.

Also, create a database in our team's Notion workspace called "Reasoning Papers" to track these papers. The database should have these properties: Title (title type), Authors (rich_text), Year (number), Method (select), Key_Contribution (rich_text), and Cited_By (number). Add an entry for each relevant reasoning paper you found.

Finally, schedule five reading group sessions on the calendar for the week of March 16 through March 20, 2026. Each session should be one hour long and cover one paper. Title them "Reading Group: [short topic]" where the topic reflects the paper being discussed, like "Reading Group: Chain-of-Thought" or "Reading Group: Tree-of-Thought". Schedule them from 10:00 to 11:00 each day, Monday through Friday. Make the 10:00-11:00 wall-clock time unambiguous by providing the event times as UTC (for example "2026-03-16T10:00:00Z" or "2026-03-16T10:00:00"), or by supplying an ISO time with a timezone offset and passing the corresponding timeZone field (for example start time "2026-03-16T10:00:00+08:00" with timeZone "Asia/Shanghai").

The guide does not identify papers, so for each literal method query `chain-of-thought prompting`, `tree of thoughts`, `self-consistency chain of thought`, `step-by-step verification`, and `automatic chain of thought`, the main agent must issue `search-arxiv(keyword=<method query>)` and `search_papers(query=<method query>,max_results=10)` as native-parallel discovery calls.    5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): One explore sub-agent receives the literal automatic chain-of-thought `{paper_id,title}` assignment, calls `read_paper(paper_id=<paper_id>)` and `search-google-scholar(keyword=<exact title>)`, and returns `{paper_id,title,authors,year,method,key_contribution,results,cited_by,evidence}`.

You are helping prepare a survey on LLM reasoning methods. Five papers have been downloaded to the local arXiv storage and are accessible via the read_paper tool. Read each of the following papers using mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper with these paper IDs:

1. 2201.11903 — "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" (Wei, Wang, Schuurmans et al.)
2. 2305.10601 — "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models" (Yao, Yu, Zhao et al.)
3. 2203.11171 — "Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models" (Wang, Wei, Schuurmans et al.)
4. 2305.20050 — "Let's Verify Step by Step" (Lightman, Kosaraju, Burda et al.)
5. 2210.03629 — "Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models" (Zhang, Zhang, Li et al.)

For EACH paper, extract and report:
- Full title and complete author list (as many as shown)
- Publication year (from the paper; note if it states a venue/year)
- Key contribution and novelty (1-3 sentences)
- Methodology / approach (how the method works, key technical ideas)
- Main experimental results and benchmarks used (datasets, key quantitative improvements over baselines, e.g. accuracy numbers)
- Approximate citation count if mentioned in the paper (unlikely, so note "not stated")
- Any stated limitations

Report back in a structured, detailed format (per paper, a few short paragraphs + bullet numbers for results). This will be used to write a survey document, a comparative table (accuracy improvement, computational cost, task generality per method), and a Notion database. Be accurate and specific with numbers and benchmark names. Do not modify any files — read-only task.
Read 5 LLM reasoning papers

Create a Word document named LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx in the directory /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_Kimi-K3/SingleUserTurn-scholarly-arxiv-survey-word-notion-gcal/workspace/ (use an absolute path). It is a literature survey on reasoning methods for large language models. Use the mcp__word__ tools: create the document, add the title, then add sections with the mcp__word__add_heading tool using EXACT heading levels as specified (level 1 for main sections, level 2 for subsections — these map to Word "Heading 1"/"Heading 2" styles), and add body text with mcp__word__add_paragraph. Add the comparative table with mcp__word__add_table and format it (header row bold/shaded via format_table or highlight_table_header).

REQUIRED DOCUMENT STRUCTURE AND CONTENT (follow exactly; you may lightly polish prose but keep all facts, numbers, section names, and order):

Title paragraph (bold, large font ~16pt, centered if possible): "A Survey of Reasoning Methods for Large Language Models"

=== Section: Abstract (Heading 1) ===
One paragraph, 150-200 words, along these lines:
"This survey provides a comprehensive overview of reasoning methods for large language models (LLMs), a rapidly evolving research area focused on eliciting, structuring, and verifying multi-step reasoning. We review five representative approaches drawn from five influential papers: chain-of-thought prompting, which elicits step-by-step reasoning traces through few-shot exemplars; automatic chain-of-thought generation (Auto-CoT), which removes the need for hand-crafted demonstrations; self-consistency decoding, which samples diverse reasoning paths and marginalizes over them via majority voting; tree-of-thought reasoning, which generalizes linear chains into deliberate tree-structured search with lookahead and backtracking; and step-by-step verification through process supervision, which trains reward models on per-step human feedback. For each method we summarize the key contribution, methodology, and principal experimental results, and we organize the methods into a taxonomy spanning prompting-based, search-based, and verification-based categories. A comparative analysis evaluates the methods along four dimensions: accuracy improvement over baselines, computational cost, task generality, and implementation complexity. Finally, we discuss open challenges—including computational overhead, annotation costs, and limited generalization—and outline promising directions for future research on reliable LLM reasoning."

=== Section: 1. Introduction (Heading 1) ===
2-3 paragraphs covering: (a) motivation — LLMs excel at many NLP tasks but struggle with multi-step arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning when prompted conventionally; reasoning methods have emerged to close this gap; (b) scope — this survey covers five representative reasoning methods from five papers (Wei et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2022; Yao et al. 2023; Lightman et al. 2023), organized into prompting-based, search-based, and verification-based categories; (c) contributions — a structured taxonomy, per-method summaries of contribution/methodology/results, a comparative analysis table, and a discussion of open challenges.

=== Section: 2. Background (Heading 1) ===
2-3 paragraphs covering: fundamentals of large language models (transformer-based autoregressive models pretrained on large text corpora; scale unlocks emergent abilities); in-context learning (conditioning on a prompt containing a few input-output exemplars without parameter updates; few-shot vs. zero-shot); and prompting paradigms (standard input-output prompting vs. rationale-augmented prompting; the role of prompt design and decoding strategies in eliciting reasoning).

=== Section: 3. Taxonomy of Methods (Heading 1) ===
Intro paragraph: explain the taxonomy groups methods into three categories: (1) prompting-based methods that elicit reasoning through prompt design (chain-of-thought, automatic chain-of-thought); (2) search-based methods that explore multiple reasoning paths (self-consistency, tree of thoughts); (3) verification-based methods that validate reasoning steps (process supervision). Each method below is covered in its own subsection.

--- Subsection: 3.1 Chain-of-Thought Prompting (Heading 2) ---
Paper: "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" by Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, et al. (2022).
Cover: (1) Key contribution — introduces chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, augmenting few-shot exemplars with intermediate reasoning steps; shows CoT is an emergent ability of sufficiently large models (~100B parameters). (2) Methodology — each exemplar in the few-shot prompt includes a natural-language chain of thought leading to the answer; the model then generates analogous reasoning traces at inference; no fine-tuning required. (3) Results — evaluated on arithmetic (GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, AQuA, MAWPS), commonsense (CSQA, StrategyQA), and symbolic reasoning benchmarks; on GSM8K, PaLM 540B with CoT reaches 56.9% vs. 17.9% with standard prompting (+39.0 points); gains appear only at large model scale.

--- Subsection: 3.2 Automatic Chain-of-Thought Generation (Heading 2) ---
Paper: "Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models" by Zhuosheng Zhang, Aston Zhang, Mu Li, et al. (2022).
Cover: (1) Key contribution — Auto-CoT automatically constructs CoT demonstrations, eliminating manual, expertise-dependent exemplar crafting while matching or exceeding manual-CoT performance. (2) Methodology — two stages: question clustering (embed dataset questions, partition with k-means, select a representative question per cluster for diversity) and demonstration generation (produce reasoning chains for selected questions with Zero-Shot-CoT, i.e., appending "Let's think step by step"); the auto-constructed demonstrations are then used for few-shot CoT prompting. (3) Results — evaluated on 10 reasoning benchmarks including MultiArith, GSM8K, and CSQA; on MultiArith, Auto-CoT reaches 92.0% vs. 91.7% for manual CoT, matching or exceeding manual prompting while removing human annotation effort; a limitation is that zero-shot-generated chains may contain errors.

--- Subsection: 3.3 Self-Consistency Decoding (Heading 2) ---
Paper: "Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models" by Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, et al. (2022).
Cover: (1) Key contribution — introduces self-consistency, a decoding strategy replacing greedy decoding in CoT prompting; motivated by the observation that complex reasoning problems admit multiple valid reasoning paths to the same answer. (2) Methodology — prompt with CoT exemplars, sample a diverse set of reasoning paths at non-zero temperature, then marginalize over the paths by taking a majority vote over final answers; fully unsupervised, no additional training. (3) Results — on GSM8K with PaLM 540B, self-consistency reaches 74.4% vs. 56.9% for standard CoT (+17.9 points); +3.9 points on ARC; accuracy improves with more sampled paths, saturating around ~40 samples; cost is increased inference compute.

--- Subsection: 3.4 Tree-of-Thought Reasoning (Heading 2) ---
Paper: "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models" by Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, et al. (2023).
Cover: (1) Key contribution — introduces Tree of Thoughts (ToT), generalizing CoT into exploration over a tree of coherent intermediate "thoughts", enabling deliberate decision-making, lookahead, and backtracking. (2) Methodology — four components: thought decomposition of the problem; thought generation (sampling or propose prompting); state evaluation (value or vote prompting, with the LM acting as its own evaluator); and tree search via BFS or DFS. (3) Results — with GPT-4 on Game of 24, ToT achieves 74% success vs. 4% for CoT; on Mini Crosswords, 60% of games solved vs. 16% for best-of-100 CoT sampling; on Creative Writing, ToT passages are judged more coherent; costs are many more LM calls per problem and the need for task-specific thought decomposition and evaluation prompts.

--- Subsection: 3.5 Step-by-Step Verification with Process Supervision (Heading 2) ---
Paper: "Let's Verify Step by Step" by Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, et al. (2023).
Cover: (1) Key contribution — investigates process supervision (feedback on each intermediate reasoning step) vs. outcome supervision (feedback only on the final answer) for training reward models that verify LLM reasoning; releases PRM800K, a dataset of 800K step-level human feedback labels. (2) Methodology — train Process Reward Models (PRMs) on human labels marking each step of model-generated solutions as correct, incorrect, or neutral; compare with Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) trained only on final-answer correctness; both act as verifiers selecting among multiple candidate solutions. (3) Results — on the MATH benchmark, PRM-based verification reaches 78.2% accuracy vs. 72.4% for ORM and 53.2% for majority voting; process supervision gives more interpretable per-step reward signals; limitation is the high cost of step-level human annotation and training a separate reward model.

=== Section: 4. Comparative Analysis (Heading 1) ===
One paragraph: summarize that the methods trade accuracy against computational cost and generality; CoT and Auto-CoT are cheap and broadly applicable; self-consistency adds sampling cost but is task-general; ToT achieves the largest gains on search-heavy problems at high inference cost and lower generality; process supervision yields the strongest verification reliability on multi-step math reasoning but requires expensive step-level annotation.
Then add a table with EXACTLY these 5 columns and header row:
Header: Method Name | Paper Title | Accuracy Improvement | Computational Cost | Task Generality
Rows:
1. Chain-of-Thought Prompting | Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models | +39.0 points on GSM8K (17.9% to 56.9%, PaLM 540B) | Low: single inference pass, few-shot prompt, no fine-tuning | Broad: arithmetic, commonsense, symbolic; requires ~100B+ models
2. Automatic Chain-of-Thought (Auto-CoT) | Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models | Matches/beats manual CoT (MultiArith 92.0% vs. 91.7%) | Low-moderate: one-time clustering plus zero-shot chain generation | Broad: validated on 10 diverse reasoning benchmarks
3. Self-Consistency | Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models | +17.9 points on GSM8K over CoT (56.9% to 74.4%); +3.9 on ARC | Moderate-high: ~40 sampled reasoning paths per question | Broad: any CoT task with aggregatable final answers
4. Tree of Thoughts | Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models | Game of 24: 4% to 74%; Mini Crosswords: 16% to 60% | High: BFS/DFS tree search with many LM generation and evaluation calls | Narrow-moderate: search/planning-style tasks; needs per-task prompt design
5. Process Supervision (PRM) | Let's Verify Step by Step | MATH: 78.2% vs. 72.4% (ORM) and 53.2% (majority voting) | High: 800K step-level human labels plus reward-model training | Primarily math and multi-step reasoning verification
Format the table with a highlighted header row and borders; auto-fit columns.

=== Section: 5. Open Challenges (Heading 1) ===
3-4 paragraphs covering: computational cost and latency (self-consistency and ToT multiply inference calls; PRMs need extra models); dependence on model scale and prompt design (CoT benefits emerge only at ~100B; ToT needs per-task thought decomposition and evaluation prompts); annotation and data costs (PRM800K shows step-level human feedback is powerful but expensive to collect; noisy zero-shot chains in Auto-CoT); limited generality and evaluation (gains concentrate on tasks with well-defined answers; hard to verify open-ended generation); future directions — combining search with learned verification, automating process supervision, improving sample efficiency, extending reasoning methods to multimodal and agentic settings.

=== Section: 6. Conclusion (Heading 1) ===
1-2 paragraphs: summarize key findings — prompting-based methods (CoT, Auto-CoT) offer low-cost, broadly applicable gains; search-based methods (self-consistency, ToT) trade compute for substantially higher accuracy; verification-based methods (process supervision) deliver the most reliable multi-step reasoning where annotation budgets allow. Practical recommendations: start with CoT/Auto-CoT, add self-consistency when compute permits, use ToT for search-heavy problems, and adopt process supervision for high-stakes multi-step reasoning. Outlook: reasoning methods will remain central to making LLMs more capable and trustworthy.

=== Section: References (Heading 1) ===
Numbered list (plain paragraphs starting with [1], [2], ...):
[1] Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, et al. "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models." arXiv:2201.11903, 2022.
[2] Zhuosheng Zhang, Aston Zhang, Mu Li, et al. "Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models." arXiv:2210.03629, 2022.
[3] Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, et al. "Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models." arXiv:2203.11171, 2022.
[4] Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, et al. "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models." arXiv:2305.10601, 2023.
[5] Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, et al. "Let's Verify Step by Step." arXiv:2305.20050, 2023.
